title: Interfaces
description: Master interface design in C#: contracts, multiple interface implementation, default interface methods, generics, and real-world patterns like dependency injection.

data.text: An interface is a contract that defines **what** a class must do, not **how** it does it. It declares method signatures, properties, events, and indexers that implementing classes must provide. In C#, interfaces are the primary tool for achieving polymorphism without inheritance, enabling flexible and testable architecture.

An interface defines a set of capabilities that a class promises to fulfill. When a class implements an interface, it guarantees that it provides all the methods and properties declared in that interface. This decouples the consumer of an interface from the concrete class that implements it, allowing you to swap implementations freely.

terms.definition: A contract that specifies method signatures and properties a class must implement.
To fulfill an interface contract by providing concrete method bodies in a class.
Treating different objects uniformly through a shared interface type.
A design pattern where dependencies are provided (injected) from outside, often via interface types.
A method with an implementation inside an interface, introduced in C# 8.0.

data.text: By convention, C# interface names start with 'I' followed by PascalCase. Interface members are implicitly public and abstract — you cannot add access modifiers or provide a body (prior to C# 8). A class implements an interface using the same colon syntax as inheritance. A class can implement multiple interfaces, solving the multiple-inheritance limitation.

data.title: Generic Interface and Implementation
data.content: A generic IRepository<T> interface implemented by a concrete SqlRepository class.

data.text: A class can implement multiple interfaces, which is the primary mechanism for achieving a form of multiple inheritance in C#. This is powerful when a class needs to fulfill multiple distinct contracts — for example, a Document class might be both IPrintable and ISerializable.

data.title: Multiple Interfaces
data.content: A Document class implementing IPrintable, ISaveable, and ICloneable simultaneously.

data.text: Prior to C# 8, interfaces could only declare method signatures — any change to an interface would break all implementing classes. C# 8 introduced default interface methods, allowing you to provide a default implementation directly in the interface. This enables safe interface evolution without forcing all implementors to update immediately.

data.title: Default Interface Method
data.content: A default implementation in an interface that all implementors inherit automatically.

data.text: The Interface Segregation Principle is the 'I' in SOLID. It states that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. Instead of one large, fat interface, split it into smaller, more specific interfaces. This makes implementations cleaner and prevents classes from being burdened with methods they don't need.

cards.title: Fat Interface (Bad)
cards.description: One large IWorker interface forcing implementors to provide unused methods.

cards.title: Segregated Interfaces (Good)
cards.description: Split IWorker into IWorkable, IFeedable, and IRechargeable.
pros: Each class implements only what it needs

data.text: Interfaces are the backbone of dependency injection (DI), a pattern where dependencies are provided from the outside rather than created internally. This makes code loosely coupled, easier to test, and simpler to extend. The ASP.NET Core built-in DI container is a common example.

data.content: Using ILogger<T> to decouple logging from business logic.

data.title: Exercise: Build a Payment Processing System
data.description: Create an IPaymentProcessor interface with ProcessPayment(decimal amount) and Refund(string transactionId) methods. Implement CreditCardProcessor and PayPalProcessor classes. Write a PaymentService that accepts IPaymentProcessor via DI and processes a list of payments.
steps: Define IPaymentProcessor with ProcessPayment() and Refund() signatures.
Implement CreditCardProcessor with a simple Console.WriteLine confirmation.
Implement PayPalProcessor with a different confirmation message.
Create PaymentService that takes IPaymentProcessor in its constructor.
Test by passing both processor types and verifying polymorphic behavior.
data.expectedOutcome: PaymentService works with any IPaymentProcessor implementation without knowing the concrete type.

items.hint: C# 8+ feature for evolving interfaces without breaking implementors.

items.question: Can an interface have fields?
items.answer: No. Interfaces can only declare method signatures, properties, events, and indexers. They cannot contain fields. Starting with C# 11, you can use static abstract members in interfaces (for generic math), but instance fields are still not allowed.

items.question: Can an interface inherit from another interface?
items.answer: Yes. An interface can extend one or more other interfaces, inheriting all their members. The implementing class must fulfill all members from the entire interface hierarchy.

items.question: Should I use abstract classes or interfaces?
items.answer: Use abstract classes when you want to share code and have closely related types. Use interfaces when you want to define a contract that unrelated types can fulfill, or when a class needs to implement multiple contracts. In modern C#, the distinction is smaller with default interface methods.

items.question: What is explicit interface implementation?
items.answer: Explicit implementation (void IPrintable.Print() { }) hides the interface method from the class's public API. The method can only be called through an interface reference. Use it when a class implements multiple interfaces with conflicting method signatures.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Interfaces define contracts — what a class does, not how.
A class can implement multiple interfaces, overcoming single-inheritance limits.
Default interface methods (C# 8+) allow safe interface evolution.
Interfaces are central to dependency injection and testable architecture.
Follow the Interface Segregation Principle — keep interfaces focused.
data.takeaway: Interfaces enable flexible, loosely-coupled design by separating 'what' from 'how'.
